arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Ho argued the phrase appropriate relief is ambiguous. He stated this ambiguity should end the legal inquiry.
Justice Scalia questioned the clarity of the statute. He noted states need clear notice of their liability.
Justice Ginsburg asked about the prison setting. She questioned whether damages are practically available in that context.
Justice Sotomayor asked if the statute includes punitive damages. She sought clarification on the type of relief available.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of a federal statute. The phrase appropriate relief creates ambiguity. Courts must decide if this wording waives state sovereign immunity. The outcome defines the boundary of state liability under federal law.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The plaintiff side wants a broad reading of the statute. They seek to allow private damages suits against states.
The state side wants a narrow reading of the statute. They seek to preserve sovereign immunity from damages.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The plaintiff argues the phrase appropriate relief is ambiguous. They contend this ambiguity ends the inquiry into state liability.
The state argues the statute lacks clear waiver language. They contend states must know their liability before joining the scheme.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg asked if damages are impossible in prison settings. She questioned the practical relevance of the legal theory.
Justice Scalia asked if the statute clearly defines state liability. He noted the word appropriate relief lacks clarity compared to other cases.
